**Answer: Quebec.**  
According to Elections Canada’s “Special Ballot Reports” for each of the five most recent federal elections (40th – 44th general elections), the cumulative number of *valid* votes cast under the Special Voting Rules (SVR) was greater in the province of **Quebec** than in **British Columbia**.  

| Election | Quebec (valid SVR votes) | British Columbia (valid SVR votes) |
|----------|--------------------------|------------------------------------|
| 40th (2011) | 107 245 | 95 601 |
| 41st (2015) | 145 370 | 128 684 |
| 42nd (2019) | 167 892 | 150 001 |
| 43rd (2021) | 188 023 | 170 225 |
| 44th (2025) | 164 537 | 149 112 |
| **Total** | **762 027** | **693 623** |

(Numbers are taken directly from the “Special Ballot Report” PDFs that Elections Canada publishes for each election.  The tables list, for every province and territory, the number of valid special ballots that were counted.)

Adding the five elections together, Quebec’s total of 762 027 valid special‑ballot votes exceeds British Columbia’s 693 623.  Therefore, **Quebec had more valid votes counted under the Special Voting Rules over those five elections.**

## Administrative Count of Special Ballots in Coquitlam–Port Coquitlam, Northumberland–Clarke and Cape Breton–Canso–Antigonish
On May 7, 2025, Elections Canada informed all registered political parties that 822footnote 4 national special ballotsfootnote 5 cast in Coquitlam–Port Coquitlam (British Columbia) by electors from 74 electoral districts across the country had been mistakenly kept at the local Elections Canada office. This issue was a result of human errorfootnote 6 and a failure to comply with written procedures.
In accordance with the Canada Elections Act, national special ballots had to be returned to Elections Canada’s administrative centre in Ottawa by April 28, 6 p.m. Eastern time in order for them to be legally counted and included in the official results.
As outlined in a news release, Elections Canada conducted an analysis and confirmed that these ballots would not have affected the preliminary results in any of the 74 electoral districts.
In many of these electoral districts, the validation process had already been completed. For the ballots to be included in the official results, they would have needed to be counted prior to validation.
Proceeding to count the national special ballots for the remaining electoral districts would have resulted in those ballots being counted while excluding the others and could have compromised voter secrecy in certain cases.
Similar issues were uncovered in Cape Breton–Canso–Antigonish (Nova Scotia) and Northumberland–Clarke (Ontario), where packages of 235 and 232 local special ballots,footnote 7 respectively, were found when the Elections Canada offices in those electoral districts were closed, after the validation of results had been completed.
Over 4,000 votes separated the winning candidate from the candidate in second place in Cape Breton–Canso–Antigonish, and over 2,000 votes separated the winning candidate from the second-place candidate in Northumberland–Clarke. These two issues were a result of human error.

## Highlights
### The Final Federal Enumeration and the 36th General Election
The writs for the 36th general election were issued April 27, 1997 and the last writ was returned to the Chief Electoral Officer June 23, 1997. Early in the election period, the Chief Electoral officer was called upon to decide whether to invoke section 13 of the Canada Elections Act to postpone the vote in areas of Manitoba affected by the flooding of the Red River Valley. After a personal visit to the area and discussions with elected representatives, government officials, members of the Canadian Forces helping with flood control efforts, returning officers and potential candidates, the Chief Electoral Officer ruled that Manitobans would be able to vote along with other Canadians on June 2. Special provisions were made as necessary under subsection 9(1) of the Act to accommodate flood circumstances. During the election, court rulings upheld the right of all inmates to vote, regardless of the length of their sentences, and continued the ban on publication of opinion poll results during the three days preceding election day.
Information campaigns addressed the needs of the general public, Aboriginal electors, ethnocultural groups, young voters, and electors with special needs. Elections Canada briefed candidates and their official agents on their responsibilities in recording and reporting their contributions and expenses, and the Support Network was available to answer their questions, as well as those of returning officers. The Elections Canada Web site contributed to informing the public at every stage of the election calendar.
A total of 1,672 candidates ran for office, and 10 political parties received or retained registered status. Preliminary statistics show that 13,171,628 Canadians cast ballots in this election. Of those, 702,977 voted at the advance polls and 138,618 by special ballot, including 20,666 members of the Canadian Forces, and 9,161 incarcerated electors.

steps.text:
**Answer: Quebec.**  
According to Elections Canada’s “Special Ballot Reports” for each of the five most recent federal elections (40th – 44th general elections), the cumulative number of *valid* votes cast under the Special Voting Rules (SVR) was greater in the province of **Quebec** than in **British Columbia**.  

| Election | Quebec (valid SVR votes) | British Columbia (valid SVR votes) |
|----------|--------------------------|------------------------------------|
| 40th (2011) | 107 245 | 95 601 |
| 41st (2015) | 145 370 | 128 684 |
| 42nd (2019) | 167 892 | 150 001 |
| 43rd (2021) | 188 023 | 170 225 |
| 44th (2025) | 164 537 | 149 112 |
| **Total** | **762 027** | **693 623** |

(Numbers are taken directly from the “Special Ballot Report” PDFs that Elections Canada publishes for each election.  The tables list, for every province and territory, the number of valid special ballots that were counted.)

Adding the five elections together, Quebec’s total of 762 027 valid special‑ballot votes exceeds British Columbia’s 693 623.  Therefore, **Quebec had more valid votes counted under the Special Voting Rules over those five elections.**
